newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists stand firm against protests.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists stand firm against protests.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists held out stubbornly against a rising chorus of protest from doctors, students, gypsies and miners on Tuesday, the eve of opposition lawyer Petar Stoyanov's installation as president.
The Socialists threatened a tougher response to the daily rallies, saying that they were under pressure from regional party groups to organise pro-government counter-rallies.

As demonstrations fuelled by economic crisis entered their third week, about 1,500 doctors gathered at the health ministry to protest at their ill-equipped hospitals and low wages and vowed to return every day until their demands were met.
Along with groups of students and gypsies, they later joined the daily gathering outside Sofia's gold-domed Orthodox cathedral, which drew around 17,000 people on Tuesday.
Ivan Kostov, leader of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), said an apology for the Socialists' past errors from party leader Georgi Parvanov on Monday was not enough.
"We have to keep on with our protests because on the one hand they are apologising but on the other hand they are still keen to form a second Socialist government," Kostov said.

The Socialists have offered elections in December, a year ahead of schedule, but want to form a second cabinet following the resignation of prime minister Zhan Videnov on December 21. The UDF wants elections in March.

Student protesters gathered for a concert in front of the mausoleum which formerly housed the remains of Bulgarian Communist hero Georgi Dimitrov. Some massed on the platform from where former communist leaders used to greet parades.
"We want not to exist but to live. We want professional fulfilment and a chance to have normal families. If we have children, Bulgaria will have a future," drama student Lili Bogdanova said.
One-hour warning strikes took place in several factories and mines around the country. Miners are demanding higher wages to keep pace with annual inflation of more than 300 percent.

"We have been humiliated by low salaries and unbearable working conditions," an associate professor from Sofia's Pirogov emergency hospital said. "It is absurd in Europe at the end of the 20th century to have patients bringing their own medicines and their own bandages to be treated in hospital."

Vassil Karinov, a member of the Socialists' executive bureau, said party leaders had met regional organisations around the country who felt the ex-communist party was not doing enough to respond to the protests.

"They insist that we must have a tougher approach against the pressure of the opposition. Our local organisations also want to organise counter-rallies to respond to the opposition protest rallies," he told a news conference.
Counter-rallies by supporters of neighbouring Serbia's Socialist President Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade on December 24 led to violent clashes between demonstrators and police.
Karinov said the Socialists insisted on forming a new cabinet until elections at the end of the year, and planned to introduce emergency economic measures in the next few weeks.
Parvanov said on Monday a new Socialist government was the only way to secure new funding from international lenders, and proposed a "clean hands" operation to purge corrupt politicians.
The party on Tuesday elected Parvanov as chairman of its parliamentary group, replacing Krassimir Premyanov, who has attracted criticism for his business connections.

Outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev has refused to ask the Socialists to form a new cabinet in the present atmosphere and both sides hope Stoyanov can help break the deadlock over formation of a new government and scheduling of elections.
